title: Kernel and image of homogeneous substitution for a quadratic formal cone
statement:
Let $F$ be a field, let $a,b,c\in F$ with $a\ne0$, and put $\beta=b/a$, $\gamma=c/a$, $p(Z)=Z^2+\beta Z+\gamma$, $q=aX^2+bXY+cY^2$, and
$$L=F[Z]/(aZ^2+bZ+c)=F[Z]/(p),\qquad B=L[[t]].$$
Here the equality of quotients uses the equality of the two principal ideals. Write $z\in L$ for the class of $Z$. Polynomial rings, formal power series, and algebra quotients are [def-weil-polynomial-ring], [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series], and [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. The scalar map $F\to L$ is injective, $1,z$ form an $F$-basis of $L$, and $z^2=-\beta z-\gamma$.
For $H=\sum_{n\ge0}H_n\in F[[X,Y]]$, where $H_n=\sum_{i=0}^n h_{i,n-i}X^iY^{n-i}$ is its homogeneous polynomial of degree $n$, the formula
$$\phi(H)=\sum_{n\ge0}H_n(z,1)t^n$$
defines an $F$-algebra homomorphism with $\phi(X)=zt$, $\phi(Y)=t$,
$$\ker\phi=(q),\qquad \operatorname{im}\phi=A:=F+tB.$$
In particular it induces an injective $F$-algebra map $j:F[[X,Y]]/(q)\to B$ with image $A$, and $F[[t]]\subseteq A$, $tB\subseteq A$. More explicitly, if
$$h=\alpha_0+\sum_{n\ge1}(\alpha_n+\delta_nz)t^n,\qquad \alpha_n,\delta_n\in F,$$
then
$$\phi\!\left(\alpha_0+\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_nY^n+\sum_{n\ge1}\delta_nXY^{n-1}\right)=h.$$
No discriminant hypothesis is required.

proof.text: Since $a$ is invertible, $aZ^2+bZ+c=ap$ generates the same ideal as $p$. Thus the two displayed quotient algebras agree [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. The polynomial $p$ is monic of degree $2$, so [lem-weil-pbc-monic-quotient-free] gives the basis $1,z$. Its linear independence implies that the scalar map is injective: a scalar $u$ maps to zero only if the coefficient $u$ of $1$ is zero [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. The image of $p$ in the quotient is zero, hence $z^2=-\beta z-\gamma$. Put $Q=X^2+\beta XY+\gamma Y^2=a^{-1}q$.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Cases I and II, and final displayed scalar-constant description; explicit homogeneous coefficient argument supplied by N9, valid also for degenerate quadratics.

proof.text: Grouping coefficients by $i+j=n$ defines $H_n$ with finitely many terms [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Each coefficient of the proposed $\phi(H)$ is therefore defined by a finite sum. Addition and scalar multiplication commute with these sums. For $H,K$, the degree-$n$ part of their product is $\sum_{r+s=n}H_rK_s$, directly by the finite convolution defining multiplication. Polynomial evaluation at $(z,1)$ is multiplicative by the same distributive calculation [def-weil-polynomial-ring]. Consequently $[t^n]\phi(HK)=\sum_{r+s=n}H_r(z,1)K_s(z,1)=[t^n](\phi(H)\phi(K))$. Constants map to their scalar images, and $\phi(X)=zt$, $\phi(Y)=t$. This proves the asserted $F$-algebra homomorphism without any interchange of infinite sums.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Cases I and II, and final displayed scalar-constant description; explicit homogeneous coefficient argument supplied by N9, valid also for degenerate quadratics.

proof.text: Here is finite homogeneous division, explicitly. For $n\ge2$, start with the polynomial $H_n$ and a zero accumulator $G_{n-2}$. Whenever the current coefficient of $X^jY^{n-j}$ is $d$ with $j\ge2$, subtract $dX^{j-2}Y^{n-j}Q$ and add $dX^{j-2}Y^{n-j}$ to the accumulator. The subtracted polynomial is $dX^jY^{n-j}+d\beta X^{j-1}Y^{n-j+1}+d\gamma X^{j-2}Y^{n-j+2}$, so it kills that coefficient and creates only smaller $X$ exponents. Processing $j=n,n-1,\ldots,2$ terminates with an identity $H_n=QG_{n-2}+u_nY^n+v_nXY^{n-1}$, with $G_{n-2}$ homogeneous of degree $n-2$. This is a finite sequence of polynomial identities [def-weil-polynomial-ring]. For $n=1$ write $H_1=u_1Y+v_1X$; for $n=0$ write $H_0=u_0$.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Cases I and II, and final displayed scalar-constant description; explicit homogeneous coefficient argument supplied by N9, valid also for degenerate quadratics.

proof.text: Suppose $\phi(H)=0$. Equality of formal-series coefficients gives $H_n(z,1)=0$ for every $n$ [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Evaluating the preceding division identities and using $Q(z,1)=0$ gives $u_n+v_nz=0$ for $n\ge1$, and $u_0=0$. The basis in [lem-weil-pbc-monic-quotient-free], interpreted by [def-weil-pbc-free-module], forces $u_n=v_n=0$. In particular $H_0=H_1=0$, and $H_n=QG_{n-2}$ for $n\ge2$. Define $G$ coefficientwise by taking its homogeneous part of degree $m$ to be the finite polynomial $G_m$ obtained in degree $m+2$; this is an element of $F[[X,Y]]$ by its definition. The degree-$n$ coefficients of $QG$ are $QG_{n-2}$ for $n\ge2$ and zero in degrees $0,1$, because $Q$ is homogeneous of degree $2$. Thus $H=QG=q(a^{-1}G)$, so $\ker\phi\subseteq(q)$. Conversely $\phi(q)=a(z^2+\beta z+\gamma)t^2=0$, and multiplicativity gives $(q)\subseteq\ker\phi$.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Cases I and II, and final displayed scalar-constant description; explicit homogeneous coefficient argument supplied by N9, valid also for degenerate quadratics.

proof.text: The constant coefficient of $\phi(H)$ is the scalar $H_0$, so its image lies in $F+tB$ [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Conversely every coefficient of any $h\in F+tB$ has a unique form $\alpha_n+\delta_nz$ by [lem-weil-pbc-monic-quotient-free] and [def-weil-pbc-free-module], with $\delta_0=0$. The series $S=\alpha_0+\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_nY^n+\sum_{n\ge1}\delta_nXY^{n-1}$ is defined coefficientwise: for each $n\ge1$ its homogeneous part has exactly the two indicated possible monomials. Hence $[t^0]\phi(S)=\alpha_0$ and $[t^n]\phi(S)=\alpha_n+\delta_nz$ for $n\ge1$. This proves the explicit formula and $\operatorname{im}\phi=F+tB$.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Cases I and II, and final displayed scalar-constant description; explicit homogeneous coefficient argument supplied by N9, valid also for degenerate quadratics.

proof.text: Define $j([H])=\phi(H)$. If $[H]=[K]$ then $H-K\in(q)=\ker\phi$, so this is well-defined; its algebra identities descend from those of $\phi$ [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. If $j([H])=0$ then $H\in\ker\phi=(q)$, so $[H]=0$; thus $j$ is injective. Surjectivity of the quotient map implies that $j$ has the same image as $\phi$, namely $A$. Any series in $F[[t]]$ has scalar constant coefficient, and every series in $tB$ has zero constant coefficient, so both lie in $A$. No step used separability, a root of $p$ in $F$, or a nonzero discriminant.
